common_name: Cherokee Long Ear Popcorn (Colorful Long-Eared Heirloom Popcorn)
scientific_name: Zea mays var. everta 'Cherokee Long Ear'

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; Cherokee Long Ear is a tall heirloom popcorn valued for its unusually long, slender ears and multicolored kernels. Isolate from sweet corn and other corn types by distance or planting-date offset to prevent cross-pollination.

directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks for reliable wind pollination; let ears dry fully on the stalk, then cure an additional few weeks indoors before shelling and popping. Cherokee Long Ear is an heirloom popcorn grown for its distinctively long, slender ears — noticeably longer than most popcorn types — filled with small kernels in a mix of colors including reds, browns, and yellows on the same ear, giving each harvest a naturally varied, decorative look. It pops into small, tender, flavorful popcorn once fully dried and cured. The tall, vigorous stalks and long ears also make it a popular choice for fall decoration and dried-corn displays in addition to eating. Harvest when husks are fully dry and kernels are hard, and test-pop a small handful before committing the full harvest to storage.

common_name: Speckled Hound Squash (Chef-Bred Sweet Delicata-Type Winter Squash)

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Speckled Hound is a modern chef-bred delicata-type squash selected for sweetness and a longer-storing, tougher rind than standard delicata.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vine plenty of room to spread. Speckled Hound was bred by Row 7 Seed Company in collaboration with chefs specifically for improved flavor over standard delicata squash, producing oblong, cream-colored fruit speckled and streaked with green, with notably sweet, dense, richly flavored orange flesh and a somewhat tougher rind that stores longer than typical delicata types. Harvest when the rind hardens and speckled coloring fully develops, usually as the vine begins to decline in late summer or fall, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to improve flavor and shelf life. Like other Cucurbita pepo squash, watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs in Gulf South gardens.

planting.note: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since habanero-type peppers are slow to germinate and establish; Habanada carries the full fruity, floral habanero aroma and flavor entirely without heat.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Habanada was bred at Cornell University and further developed by Row 7 Seed Company by selecting for the characteristic fruity, floral, tropical habanero flavor and aroma while breeding out the capsaicin that gives habaneros their intense heat, resulting in a pepper that tastes like a habanero but can be eaten fresh in quantity without any burn. Small, lantern-shaped fruits ripen from green to a bright golden-orange, and the plant is productive over a long season much like a standard habanero. It is excellent fresh in salsas, salads, and sauces where habanero flavor is wanted without the heat. Harvest at the fully ripe orange stage for the strongest flavor, and expect steady production through summer into fall.

planting.note: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Koginut is a cross between kabocha and butternut squash bred by Row 7 Seed Company in collaboration with chef Dan Barber, selected for a rich, dense, exceptionally sweet flesh.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the vigorous vine room to sprawl. Koginut combines the deep, nutty sweetness and dry, dense texture of kabocha squash with the smoother shape and easier peeling of butternut, developed through a chef-driven breeding collaboration specifically to concentrate flavor rather than yield or shelf appearance. The tan, ribbed, acorn-shaped fruit has an intensely sweet, richly flavored orange flesh that roasts especially well. Harvest when the rind hardens and dulls to a matte tan color, usually as the vine declines in late summer or fall, and cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to further concentrate sweetness. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common problems for cucurbits in Gulf South gardens.

common_name: Badger Flame Beet (Sweet Low-Earthiness Orange Beet)

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop; Badger Flame was bred by Row 7 Seed Company and the University of Wisconsin specifically to minimize the earthy geosmin flavor many people dislike in beets.

directions: Direct sow seed clusters a half-inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once they emerge, since each beet seed cluster produces several sprouts. Badger Flame was bred through a collaboration between Row 7 Seed Company and University of Wisconsin plant breeders specifically to reduce the earthy geosmin compound responsible for the polarizing 'dirt' flavor many people associate with beets, resulting in roots with a notably sweet, mild flavor and a distinctive flame-like pattern of yellow and red rings when sliced. Its mild sweetness holds up well eaten raw, shaved thin, or roasted, appealing to cooks and diners who normally avoid beets. Keep soil consistently moist for even root development, and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best texture and flavor.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison vegetable breeding program
